newsitem.title: DUBAI: Anti-German Iran marchers say ready for martyrdom.
newsitem.headline: Anti-German Iran marchers say ready for martyrdom.

text.p: The leader of a hardline Islamist Iranian group said on Friday his followers were ready to die as martyrs against Germany if ordered by Iran's supreme leader, residents said.

Hossein Allahkaram, leader of the Ansar-e Hizbollah, told a rally of about 1,000 people at the German embassy in Tehran that many members were willing to sacrifice their lives in actions against German interests if ordered by Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Allahkaram, who is known for his fiery rhetoric, did not say which kinds of actions.

The rally was the latest protest against a German court's verdict accusing Iranian leaders of ordering the 1992 killings of four Kurdish dissidents in Berlin. Iran has denied any role in the slayings.
"We advise the Germans to shake off America's domination," Allahkaram told protesters.

The protesters had marched to the German embassy from Friday prayers chanting slogans against Israel and the United States, which they blamed for provoking the row between Iran and Germany, until recently Tehran's main trade partner.

They joined some 200 veterans disabled by Iraqi chemical attacks in the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq war who were staging a sit-in outside the embassy to back demands to prosecute German firms accused of supplying toxic chemicals to Baghdad.
The veterans later ended their three-day sit-in after senior officials sent messages promising to follow up a lawsuit against the firms, the Iranian news agency IRNA said.
Ansar-e Hizbollah is a group of Islamis zealots who have attacked bookstores selling literature seen as immoral and disrupted meetings of liberal opposition groups.
Iranian officials have said they are committed to protecting foreign residents and Bonn has said it had no reason to doubt the 530 Germans in Iran were safe.
Iran's head of judiciary Ayatollah Mohammad Yazdi said on Friday Tehran had almost completed preparation for the lawsuit against the German companies.

"The lawsuit's investigations are 90 percent complete and it is ready to be brought to court against 24 German firms...four of their managers, and certain German officials who authorised these substances to be exported to Iraq from Germany," Yazdi said at Friday prayers.
Iran, which had raised the accusations as far back as 1987, said it was reactivating the case last year amid tensions with Germany over the Berlin trial.
